1380.title: Work as worship
1380.hook: kirat, honest labor, is itself devotion
1380.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of kirat karni, earning an honest living by one's own work, as part of the path alongside remembering the Name and sharing, and tell the story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago to show it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, grihasth, the householder's path: the lotus in the pond, spotless in the soot. Your line: holiness at home. A new week starts.

Two dinner invitations arrive on the same evening. One comes from a carpenter named Lalo, a poor man who works with his hands. His table has coarse bread. The other comes from Malik Bhago, a rich official throwing a grand feast, who expects the holy man in town to attend. The janamsakhis say Guru Nanak stayed with Lalo and didn't go to the feast. Bhago was offended, and demanded to know why. You heard this story in year one. Today it carries an idea.
screen: `TWO DINNER INVITATIONS.` → `A CARPENTER'S BREAD. A RICH MAN'S FEAST.` → `THE GURU STAYS WITH LALO.`

segments.voice: The tradition says Guru Nanak took a piece of Lalo's coarse bread in one hand and a piece of Bhago's rich food in the other, and squeezed. From Lalo's bread came milk. From Bhago's came blood. The point lands without a speech: one meal was earned by honest hands; the other was squeezed out of other people. That's kirat: honest work, earning a living by your own effort without cheating anyone. We met it beside the farmer who can't make it rain, named alongside remembering the Name and sharing. Today it gets its own story. In a salok, Guru Nanak puts it in a line. In paraphrase: the one who eats what they have earned by their own work, and gives some of it from their hand, Nanak, that one recognizes the path. Notice the order. First the earning. The path is recognized in the work, not only in the temple. Why can work be worship? If freedom can come while laughing and eating, as Guru Arjan said three days ago, it can come at a workbench too. Fixing a sink, teaching a class, stocking shelves, driving a delivery route, caring for a patient at night: done honestly, each is a kind of devotion. Not because the job is holy in itself, but because honesty in it is a way of remembering the One. Lalo's bread was ordinary. What made it sweet was how it was earned. Work is worship.
screen: `LALO'S BREAD AND BHAGO'S FEAST.` · `KIRAT: HONEST WORK.` · `EAT WHAT YOU EARN, GIVE FROM YOUR HAND.` · `THE WORKBENCH AS A PLACE OF PRAYER.` · then, large: `WORK IS WORSHIP.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the next piece of work in front of you, paid or unpaid, a report, a shift, homework, laundry, a repair, and picture doing it all the way through without one shortcut you'd be embarrassed to explain. No padding the hours, no blaming someone else, no cutting the corner nobody would see. Notice how that feels in the body, and if you pray, offer the work with Waheguru.
Work as worship. Kirat, honest work, earned by your own effort, which Sikh teaching treats as devotion itself. Today's word.
Your line: work is worship. Honest bread, honestly earned, gives milk in the story. See you tomorrow.

1381.title: Wealth, earned and shared
1381.hook: money is not evil; clinging to it and hoarding it are
1381.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of vand chhakna, sharing what one earns, and tradition describes dasvandh, setting aside a share of income, for the community and those in need, including the langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, work as worship: Lalo's bread and Bhago's feast, and kirat, honest work. Your line: work is worship.

Is money bad? Ask that at a dinner table and watch it split. Somebody says money ruins everything it touches. Somebody else says try paying rent with good intentions. Both have a point, and both are a little stuck. Honest work, done well, sometimes earns more than bread. A shop does well. A farm has a good year. A salary goes up. Then the question isn't how to earn. It's what to do with what you've earned, and what it starts doing to you.
screen: `IS MONEY BAD?` → `THE TABLE SPLITS.` → `WHAT DO YOU DO WITH WHAT YOU EARN?`

segments.voice: Money isn't the enemy. The salok we met yesterday honors the one who eats what they earn by their own work. Sikh life has room for farms, shops, businesses and savings; the householder needs a roof. So where does the trouble start? In Raag Asa, in hymns tradition links to Babar's invasion, Guru Nanak looks at wealth with clear eyes. In paraphrase: for the sake of this wealth, many were ruined and disgraced; it isn't piled up without wrongdoing, and it doesn't go along with anyone when they die. The problem isn't the coin. It's the clinging, the piling up, the wealth that has to be guarded and that guards you back. Now the other half of yesterday's line. That salok doesn't stop at earning. It says: and gives some of it from their hand. The hand that earns is meant to open. Sikhs call this sharing vand chhakna, and tradition adds dasvandh, setting aside a tenth share of what you earn for the community and for those in need; you met it in year one. Gifts like this can help feed the langar. Earning without sharing tightens the fist. Sharing without honest earning gives away what was never yours. Together, money moves through a life instead of sitting on it. A hand that earns and then opens isn't owned by what it holds. Earned and shared.
screen: `EARNING IS NOT SHAMEFUL.` · `IT DOESN'T GO ALONG AT DEATH.` · `THE HAND THAT EARNS SHOULD OPEN.` · `MONEY MOVES THROUGH, NOT SITS ON.` · then, large: `EARNED AND SHARED.`

segments.voice: Hold the picture of what you earned or received this week without adding it up, and think of one place a little of it could go that isn't you: a food bank, a gurdwara's langar, a neighbor who's short this month. Rest your hand open on your lap while you breathe, and notice what it feels like to plan to let go of something. If you pray, hold the gift with Waheguru.
Wealth. Not evil in itself; earned honestly, it is meant to be shared, and it does not go along with anyone at the end. Today's word.
Your line: earned and shared. The hand that earns is meant to open. Go gently.

1382.title: One row on the langar floor
1382.hook: caste, gender and race do not measure the soul
1382.carry: the same light in every soul
1382.howItsDone: In the gurdwara's langar, Sikhs and guests sit together in rows called pangat and are served the same food, whatever their background; anyone may serve.

segments.voice: Yesterday, wealth: not evil in itself, only in the clinging and the hoarding. Your line was earned and shared.

A long strip of cloth runs down the floor of a gurdwara hall. People sit on it in a row, shoulder to shoulder. A banker in a good coat. A student with a backpack at her feet. A man who came in off the street because he was hungry. A grandmother who barely speaks the language of the room. Someone walks down the line with a bucket of dal and fills every plate from the same ladle. Nobody's plate is first because of who they are. That row is the pangat, and it's a plain picture of today's idea.
screen: `ONE STRIP OF CLOTH. ONE ROW.` → `THE SAME LADLE FOR EVERY PLATE.` → `PANGAT.`

segments.voice: First, the light. Early on this path you met Guru Nanak's line from Raag Asa; here it is again, in paraphrase: recognize the Lord's light in everyone, and don't ask about caste; in the world beyond, there is no caste. The question a whole society used to sort people, what family were you born into, gets set aside. Not because birth is a secret, but because it measures the wrong thing. Second, a sharp question from a weaver. The Granth keeps the verses of Kabir, a weaver by trade, and in one he turns to a man proud of high birth. In paraphrase: if you are so different, why didn't you come into the world some other way? Everyone arrives the same way. The joke has a point. Third, one human family. In the Akal Ustat, a work Sikhs keep in the Dasam Granth, a line Sikhs quote says, in paraphrase: recognize the whole human race as one. Caste, gender, color, nation: none of them is the scale a soul is weighed on. Fourth, the floor. The Gurus didn't leave this a nice sentence. Sit in the row. Eat from the same pot. Take the ladle and serve whoever is next. In the langar, equality stops being an idea and becomes dinner. And equal souls isn't a claim that everyone is the same. The banker and the hungry man are still different people. The light in each is the same light.
screen: `ASA: SEE THE LIGHT, NOT THE CASTE.` · `KABIR: WE ALL ARRIVE THE SAME WAY.` · `ONE HUMAN RACE.` · `PANGAT: THE TEACHING ON THE FLOOR.` · then, large: `THE SAME LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you tend to rank, a little above you or a little below: a boss, maybe, or someone who serves you lunch. On the in-breath, see their face; on the out-breath, let the ranking drop, the way a coat slips off a chair. Then picture one ordinary way to treat them as an equal: their name used, their eyes met, their opinion asked.
Equal souls. Caste, gender and race don't measure the soul; the same light is in everyone, and the langar row puts it into practice. Today's word.
Your line: the same light in every soul. Not who are they, but where is the light in them. See you tomorrow.

1383.title: Women in the teaching
1383.hook: the Gurus honored women as equals, as teachers and as leaders
1383.howItsDone: In gurdwaras women and men can lead kirtan, read from the Guru Granth Sahib and serve in the langar; Sikhs remember women such as Mata Khivi, Mata Gujri and Mai Bhago.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the langar row: one strip of cloth, one ladle, the same light in everyone. Your line was equal souls.

Why call her bad? The question comes from Guru Nanak, in the middle of a long hymn. Around him, a woman could be treated as a lesser thing: unclean at certain times, blamed for misfortune, expected in some places to follow her husband into the fire when he died. Guru Nanak doesn't start with a rule. He starts with the plain facts of a life. Who carries the child? Who is a man engaged to, married to, befriended by? Who keeps the family going when someone dies? And then the question lands: why call her bad, from whom kings are born?
screen: `WHY CALL HER BAD?` → `THE PLAIN FACTS OF A LIFE.` → `FROM WHOM KINGS ARE BORN.`

segments.voice: First, the hymn. It sits in Asa di Var, the morning hymn sung in gurdwaras. In paraphrase: from woman we are born, in woman we are conceived, to woman we are engaged and married; through woman the generations go on. So why call her bad, from whom kings are born? It's an argument from the kitchen table, not from a throne. Second, a woman at the hearth. The Granth keeps a hymn by the bards Balwand and Satta praising Mata Khivi, the wife of Guru Angad. In paraphrase: Khivi was good, her shade cool and leafy, and she gave out rich sweet rice to all. Tradition remembers her running the Guru's langar, so the kitchen where yesterday's equality became dinner had a woman at its center. Third, a custom refused. You met this early on the path, with the manjis. Guru Amar Das speaks against the burning of widows; in paraphrase from a salok: those who burn with their husband's body are not truly sati; the true ones live on in love and goodness. Tradition also says he appointed women among the teachers he sent out. Fourth, leaders. Sikh memory holds Mata Gujri, mother of Guru Gobind Singh, steady through the hardest days, and Mai Bhago, who tradition says rallied men who had turned back and rode out with them. Teachers, cooks, mothers, leaders. And it's honest to add: the teaching is clear, and living up to it in every gurdwara and family is still a work in progress.
screen: `ASA DI VAR: WHY CALL HER BAD?` · `MATA KHIVI AT THE LANGAR.` · `GURU AMAR DAS REFUSES THE PYRE.` · `MATA GUJRI, MAI BHAGO.` · then, large: `EQUALS.`

1384.title: Force as the last resort
1384.hook: peace first; force only when every other means has failed
1384.howItsDone: Sikhs point to the Zafarnama's teaching that force is right only when all other means have failed; initiated Sikhs wear the kirpan as a sign of the duty to protect.

segments.voice: Yesterday, women in the teaching: why call her bad, from whom kings are born? Your line was equals.

A letter in Persian verse, sent to an emperor. The man who wrote it had lost his father to that empire's executioner, and had lost his sons too. He had every reason to write in pure rage. Instead the letter does something slower. It reminds the emperor of oaths he swore and broke. It talks about God, and about what a ruler owes the people. And in the middle comes one line Sikhs still carry, about when a sword may be lifted at all. The letter is the Zafarnama, from Guru Gobind Singh, and you met it early on this path. Today, that one line, up close.
screen: `A LETTER IN PERSIAN VERSE.` → `TO AN EMPEROR WHO BROKE HIS OATHS.` → `ONE LINE ABOUT THE SWORD.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In paraphrase, the Zafarnama says: when every other means has been tried and has failed, then it is right to take the sword in hand. Notice the order. The sword is not the first word. It's what's left when the other words have run out. Second, what comes before it: talking, bargaining, promises taken in good faith, patience. Tradition says the Guru's side had trusted sworn oaths before they were broken. The letter isn't a war cry; it's a reckoning, and its first weapon is the truth said plainly to power. Third, the person who holds the sword. A salok of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Guru's father, near the very end of the Granth, says in paraphrase: the one who frightens no one, and is frightened of no one, is the wise one. Not frightened: the courage to stand. Frightening no one: no taste for bullying, no swagger. Initiated Sikhs carry the kirpan, the small sword, as a sign of that pairing, and Sikhs explain it as a duty to protect, not a license to threaten. Fourth, an ordinary Tuesday. Most days nobody reaches for a sword. But the order still applies to a raised voice, a cutting email, a slammed door. Peace first, talk first, truth first, plainly said. The hard part is honesty about the word every. It's easy to say you tried everything after trying one thing twice.
screen: `ZAFARNAMA: ONLY WHEN ALL ELSE FAILS.` · `FIRST: WORDS, PATIENCE, TRUTH.` · `FRIGHTEN NONE, FEAR NONE.` · `THE ORDER ON AN ORDINARY DAY.` · then, large: `PEACE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one conflict that's live for you right now, big or small, and notice the part of you that wants to swing first. Then, breath by breath, list the gentler ways still untried: a calmer conversation, a question instead of a charge, a letter rather than a shout, a third person to help. Let one of them settle as the next step.
Force as the last resort. The Zafarnama's teaching that the sword is lifted only when every other means has failed; frighten no one, fear no one. Today's word.
screen: `FORCE AS THE LAST RESORT — today's word`.

1385.title: Justice for all
1385.hook: the good of all includes standing for the wronged
1385.howItsDone: Sikhs end the ardas with sarbat da bhala, the good of all, and remember Guru Nanak's Babarvani hymns as a protest against the suffering of ordinary people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Zafarnama: force only when every other means has failed. Your line was peace first.

The Sikh ardas, the standing prayer at the end of a service, closes on a wish for the whole world. Tere bhane sarbat da bhala: in your will, the good of all. Not the good of Sikhs. Not the good of the people in the room. Everyone. It's a lovely wish to say aloud, and a hard one to mean. Because once the good of all is the goal, someone being trampled is no longer somebody else's business. Guru Nanak once watched a city being trampled, and what he said about it is where today begins.
screen: `SARBAT DA BHALA: THE GOOD OF ALL.` → `NOT JUST US. EVERYONE.` → `A CITY TRAMPLED.`

segments.voice: First, the cry. When Babur's armies swept in, Guru Nanak, tradition says, saw the slaughter with his own eyes. His hymns about it are called the Babarvani. In one, in Raag Asa, he speaks straight to God. In paraphrase: such suffering, such crying out, and did You feel no pain? He describes women whose hair was once braided for weddings, now dragged and shamed. A hymn can be a protest. Second, naming it plainly. In Raag Tilang he calls the invading host a wedding party of sin, and says he will speak the word of truth, because the time for truth has come. No flattery of the powerful. Justice starts with refusing to call a wrong anything else. Third, the good of all. If sarbat da bhala is real, it includes the people being wronged, and it lays a claim on whoever sees it. Sikh memory keeps stories, from the Gurus to the Khalsa, of standing up for people who weren't their own. Fourth, the small stakes. Few of us will ever face an army. But someone is talked over in a meeting. Someone gets the cruel nickname. Someone's rent goes unfixed because they won't complain. Standing for them might mean a word, a witness, a phone call, a seat beside them. Guru Nanak had no army to send. He had a hymn, and he sang it.

Justice for all. Sarbat da bhala, the good of all, includes standing for the wronged, as Guru Nanak did when he cried out against Babur's slaughter. Today's word.
Your line: stand for others. One true sentence on someone's behalf is within anyone's reach. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1386.title: Other paths
1386.hook: the Gurus respected sincere seekers of every path and defended their freedom
1386.howItsDone: The Guru Granth Sahib includes hymns by Bhagats from Hindu and Muslim backgrounds, such as Kabir and Sheikh Farid; Sikhs remember Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom as a defense of the freedom of religion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Babarvani and sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Your line was stand for others.

Open the Guru Granth Sahib toward its last pages and you meet a name that isn't a Guru's: Sheikh Farid, a Sufi, a Muslim mystic, his verses kept right there in the Sikh scripture. Elsewhere you find Kabir the weaver, Namdev the calico printer, Ravidas the leatherworker. Their hymns sit beside the Gurus' own and are bowed to in the same way. That alone says something about how the Gurus saw people on other paths. But they went further than keeping their words. One Guru gave his life for people whose path was not his own.
screen: `SHEIKH FARID IN THE GRANTH.` → `KABIR, NAMDEV, RAVIDAS.` → `A GURU WHO GAVE HIS LIFE FOR OTHERS.`

segments.voice: First, the voices kept. You met the Bhagats early on this path: saints from Hindu and Muslim backgrounds whose hymns the Granth gathers beside the Gurus'. What it keeps is their devotion, not their birth or their label. Second, the living, not the label. In a salok in Majh ki Var, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: it's hard to be called a Muslim; only one who truly is one should be called that. Then he describes truly being one: the way of the saints sweet to you, pride scraped away like rust, kindness to all. He doesn't mock the faith. He sets its bar high, from inside its own words. Third, a freedom defended. Guru Gobind Singh's Bachitar Natak says of his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur, in paraphrase: he protected their tilak and their sacred thread. Sikhs remember that Kashmiri Pandits, Hindus under pressure to convert, came to the Guru for help, and that he went to Delhi and was executed there. Sikhs don't wear the tilak or the thread. He died for other people's right to wear them. Fourth, the week. Work as worship. Wealth earned and shared. Equal souls. Women as equals. Peace first. Stand for others. Each one widens the circle. Respect the sincere isn't saying every path is identical, and it isn't keeping score. It's noticing a person who truly seeks, and honoring that, whatever name they pray in.
screen: `THE BHAGATS' HYMNS KEPT IN THE GRANTH.` · `MAJH: HARD TO TRULY BE A MUSLIM.` · `GURU TEGH BAHADUR: THEIR THREAD, THEIR TILAK.` · `A WEEK THAT WIDENS THE CIRCLE.` · then, large: `RESPECT THE SINCERE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose path is different from yours: a coworker who fasts, a neighbor who goes to services, a friend who prays in another language, or one who doesn't pray at all and still searches. Breathe in and see their sincerity, the early mornings, the questions they carry. Breathe out and let your respect for it be quiet and real.
Other paths. The Gurus kept the hymns of saints from other backgrounds in the Granth, and Guru Tegh Bahadur died defending the freedom of people whose path was not his. Today's word.
Your line: respect the sincere. The circle keeps widening. See you on the path tomorrow.
